claim: Gamma synchronization increases during movement and scales with kinematic parameters.
source: Gamma synchronization increases during movement and scales with kinematic parameters.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise for the study.

claim: Subthalamic gamma power peaked in the sensorimotor part of the subthalamic nucleus in 16 patients undergoing deep brain stimulation surgery.
source: In 16 patients undergoing deep brain stimulation surgery, movements of different velocities revealed that subthalamic gamma power peaked in the sensorimotor part of the subthalamic nucleus
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data from 16 patients.

claim: Subthalamic gamma power correlated positively with maximal velocity.
source: In 16 patients undergoing deep brain stimulation surgery, movements of different velocities revealed that subthalamic gamma power peaked in the sensorimotor part of the subthalamic nucleus, correlated positively with maximal velocity
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Subthalamic gamma power correlated negatively with symptom severity.
source: In 16 patients undergoing deep brain stimulation surgery, movements of different velocities revealed that subthalamic gamma power peaked in the sensorimotor part of the subthalamic nucleus, correlated positively with maximal velocity and negatively with symptom severity.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: The effects of gamma power on movement rely on movement-related bursts of transient synchrony in the gamma band.
source: These effects relied on movement-related bursts of transient synchrony in the gamma band.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The gamma burst rate highly correlated with averaged power.
source: The gamma burst rate highly correlated with averaged power

claim: Gamma burst rate increased gradually with larger movements.

evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Gamma burst rate correlated with symptom severity.
source: The gamma burst rate highly correlated with averaged power, increased gradually with larger movements and correlated with symptom severity.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: In the dopamine-depleted state, gamma power significantly decreased.
source: In the dopamine-depleted state, gamma power and burst rate significantly decreased
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data comparing ON and OFF medication states.

claim: In the dopamine-depleted state, gamma burst rate significantly decreased.
source: In the dopamine-depleted state, gamma power and burst rate significantly decreased
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data comparing ON and OFF medication states.

claim: The decrease in gamma power and burst rate in the dopamine-depleted state was particularly pronounced when peak velocity was slower than ON medication.
source: In the dopamine-depleted state, gamma power and burst rate significantly decreased, particularly when peak velocity was slower than ON medication.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data comparing ON and OFF medication states.

claim: Burst amplitude was unaffected by the medication state.
source: Burst amplitude and duration were unaffected by the medication state.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data comparing ON and OFF medication states.

claim: Burst duration was unaffected by the medication state.
source: Burst amplitude and duration were unaffected by the medication state.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data comparing ON and OFF medication states.

claim: Insufficient recruitment of fast gamma bursts during movement may underlie bradykinesia as one of the cardinal symptoms in Parkinson's disease.
source: We propose that insufficient recruitment of fast gamma bursts during movement may underlie bradykinesia as one of the cardinal symptoms in Parkinson's disease.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Oscillatory brain rhythms contribute to the processing and long-range transmission of information through coherence of neuronal assemblies.
source: Oscillatory brain rhythms are thought to contribute to the processing and long-range transmission of information as encoded in single-neuron activity through coherence of neuronal assemblies (Fries, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fries, 2015.

claim: Pathological oscillatory patterns can be related to disease-specific symptoms in Parkinson's disease using invasive recordings in patients undergoing deep brain stimulation surgery.
source: Pathological oscillatory patterns could be related to disease-specific symptoms in Parkinson's disease using invasive recordings in patients undergoing deep brain stimulation surgery for severe movement disorders (Deuschl et al., 2006; Dams et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deuschl et al., 2006 and Dams et al., 2016.

claim: Elevated synchronization in the subthalamic beta band activity is found in Parkinson's disease.
source: Most strikingly, an elevated synchronization in the subthalamic beta band activity is found in Parkinson's disease that correlates with symptom severity in the dopamine-depleted state (Williams et al., 2003; Neumann et al., 2016b; Kühn and Volkmann, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Williams et al., 2003; Neumann et al., 2016b; Kühn and Volkmann, 2017.

claim: Elevated subthalamic beta band activity correlates with symptom severity in the dopamine-depleted state in Parkinson's disease.
source: Most strikingly, an elevated synchronization in the subthalamic beta band activity is found in Parkinson's disease that correlates with symptom severity in the dopamine-depleted state (Williams et al., 2003; Neumann et al., 2016b; Kühn and Volkmann, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Williams et al., 2003; Neumann et al., 2016b; Kühn and Volkmann, 2017.

claim: Elevated subthalamic beta band activity is attenuated by dopaminergic replacement therapy.
source: an elevated synchronization in the subthalamic beta band activity is found in Parkinson's disease that correlates with symptom severity in the dopamine-depleted state (Williams et al., 2003; Neumann et al., 2016b; Kühn and Volkmann, 2017) and is attenuated by dopaminergic replacement therapy (Kühn et al., 2006, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kühn et al., 2006, 2009.

claim: Elevated subthalamic beta band activity is attenuated by deep brain stimulation.
source: an elevated synchronization in the subthalamic beta band activity is found in Parkinson's disease that correlates with symptom severity in the dopamine-depleted state (Williams et al., 2003; Neumann et al., 2016b; Kühn and Volkmann, 2017) and is attenuated by dopaminergic replacement therapy (Kühn et al., 2006, 2009) as well as deep brain stimulation (Eusebio et al., 2011; de Hemptinne et al., 2015; Oswal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eusebio et al., 2011; de Hemptinne et al., 2015; Oswal et al., 2016.

claim: Ongoing movement is accompanied by increases in cortical gamma (30–90 Hz) oscillations in the human motor system.
source: In the human motor system, ongoing movement is accompanied by increases in cortical (Crone et al., 1998; Cheyne, 2013) and subcortical gamma (30–90 Hz) oscillations (Androulidakis et al., 2007; Kempf et al., 2009; Brücke et al., 2012, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crone et al., 1998; Cheyne, 2013.

claim: Ongoing movement is accompanied by increases in subcortical gamma (30–90 Hz) oscillations in the human motor system.
source: In the human motor system, ongoing movement is accompanied by increases in cortical (Crone et al., 1998; Cheyne, 2013) and subcortical gamma (30–90 Hz) oscillations (Androulidakis et al., 2007; Kempf et al., 2009; Brücke et al., 2012, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Androulidakis et al., 2007; Kempf et al., 2009; Brücke et al., 2012, 2013.

claim: Ongoing movement is accompanied by strengthening of coupling in the gamma frequency range in the human motor system.
source: In the human motor system, ongoing movement is accompanied by increases in cortical (Crone et al., 1998; Cheyne, 2013) and subcortical gamma (30–90 Hz) oscillations (Androulidakis et al., 2007; Kempf et al., 2009; Brücke et al., 2012, 2013) and strengthening of coupling in that frequency range (Litvak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Litvak et al., 2012.

claim: Cortical and subcortical movement-related gamma band synchronization is a general and physiological phenomenon irrespective of the underlying disease.
source: Cortical and subcortical movement-related gamma band synchronization seems a general and physiological phenomenon irrespective of the underlying disease.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the literature reviewed.

claim: The power increase in high frequencies most likely relies on mechanistically different phenomena with a primarily oscillatory component in the frequency range 30–90 Hz and overlapping asynchronous spiking activity in frequencies >100 Hz.
source: The power increase in high frequencies most likely relies on mechanistically different phenomena with a primarily oscillatory component in the frequency range 30–90 Hz and overlapping asynchronous spiking activity in frequencies >100 Hz (Fries et al., 2007; Manning et al., 2009; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fries et al., 2007; Manning et al., 2009; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012.

claim: Narrowband increases in gamma oscillations with a center frequency between 30–90 Hz and ~20 Hz width are of functional significance in encoding of movement parameters.
source: Previous studies have shown that narrowband increases in gamma oscillations with a center frequency between 30–90 Hz and ~20 Hz width were of functional significance in encoding of movement parameters (Jenkinson et al., 2012; Joundi et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jenkinson et al., 2012; Joundi et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2015.

claim: The basal ganglia play a major role in scaling of movement.
source: In line with this, human and animal studies have implicated that the basal ganglia play a major role in scaling of movement (Desmurget et al., 2003; Kravitz et al., 2010; Grafton and Tunik, 2011; Brücke et al., 2012; Joundi et al., 2012; Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Desmurget et al., 2003; Kravitz et al., 2010; Grafton and Tunik, 2011; Brücke et al., 2012; Joundi et al., 2012; Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015; Tan et al., 2015.

claim: The loss of physiological basal ganglia activity may lead to hypo- or hyperkinetic movement disorders.
source: The loss of their physiological activity may lead to hypo- or hyperkinetic movement disorders.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the role of basal ganglia in movement.

claim: Task-specific and resting state oscillatory synchronization occur in bursts rather than as continuous activity.
source: Moreover, recent studies have highlighted that both task-specific and resting state oscillatory synchronization do not reflect a continuous activity but rather occur in bursts.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from recent studies.

claim: Beta activity in the basal ganglia occurs in bursts.
source: While this has been primarily shown for beta activity in the basal ganglia (Feingold et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feingold et al., 2015.

claim: Intracerebral recordings of cortical areas show encoding capacity through variations of gamma burst density in memory processing.
source: intracerebral recordings of cortical areas highlighted an encoding capacity through variations of gamma burst density in memory processing (Kucewicz et al., 2017; Lundqvist et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kucewicz et al., 2017; Lundqvist et al., 2016.

claim: In Parkinson's disease, there is a disadvantageous distribution toward long beta bursts.
source: In Parkinson's disease, there is emerging evidence for a disadvantageous distribution toward long beta bursts (Tinkhauser et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tinkhauser et al., 2017.

claim: Movement-induced gamma oscillations drive the motor cortex.
source: We hypothesized that movement-induced gamma oscillations that have been shown to drive the motor cortex (Litvak et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Litvak et al., 2012.

claim: Movement-induced gamma oscillations are gradually scaled by kinematic velocity in the globus pallidus internus.
source: We hypothesized that movement-induced gamma oscillations that have been shown to drive the motor cortex (Litvak et al., 2012) are gradually scaled by kinematic velocity as seen in the upstream globus pallidus internus (Brücke et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brücke et al., 2012.

claim: The globus pallidus internus is the main projection-target of the subthalamic nucleus and major output nucleus of the basal ganglia.
source: the upstream globus pallidus internus (Brücke et al., 2012), the main projection-target of the subthalamic nucleus and major output nucleus of the basal ganglia.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Reaction time was significantly shorter in the small compared to the medium and large condition in the patient cohort ON medication (n = 16).

source: Patients were not significantly slower in the OFF compared to the ON state (n = 7, p=0.1) when averaged across all conditions

claim: Patients in the OFF-dopaminergic state were primarily impaired in the execution of large and fast movements, while smaller and respective slower movements were less affected without dopaminergic replacement therapy.
source: This indicates that patients in the OFF-dopaminergic state were primarily impaired in the execution of large and fast movements, while smaller and respective slower movements were less affected without dopaminergic replacement therapy.

source: In all conditions, movement onset was preceded and accompanied by an ERS in the theta frequency range (2 to 8 Hz) and an ERD in the beta band (13 to 30 Hz).

claim: Gamma power around maximal velocity showed a stepwise increase with movement velocity in both hemispheres (contralateral: small: 5.7%, medium: 9.4%, large: 11.6%, small vs large, p<0.001, small vs medium, p<0.001, medium vs large, p=0.02; ipsilateral: small: 4.1%, medium: 7.2%, large: 9.4%, small vs large, p=0.004, small versus medium, p=0.004, medium versus large, p=0.01).
source: Permutation testing of averaged time-frequency bands revealed a stepwise increase of gamma power with movement velocity in both hemispheres (contralateral: small: 5.7%, medium: 9.4%, large: 11.6%, small vs large, p<0.001, small vs medium, p<0.001, medium vs large, p=0.02; ipsilateral: small: 4.1%, medium: 7.2%, large: 9.4%, small vs large, p=0.004, small versus medium, p=0.004, medium versus large, p=0.01; FDR-corrected), see Figure 2.

claim: No modulation by movement condition was seen in the theta or beta band.

claim: Parametric movement-related modulation of oscillatory activity in the contralateral hemisphere was essentially restricted to the gamma band, ranging from 32 to 100 Hz in a period of up to 2.7 s after movement onset.
source: Direct comparison of relative power changes in all time-frequency bins across movement conditions (large, medium or small movement) confirmed a parametric movement-related modulation of oscillatory activity in the contralateral hemisphere that was essentially restricted to the gamma band, ranging from 32 to 100 Hz in a period of up to 2.7 s after movement onset.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical comparison of time-frequency data.

claim: Movement-related changes in oscillatory activity were seen in both the ipsi- and the contralateral subthalamic nucleus to the moved side.
source: Movement-related changes in oscillatory activity were seen in both the ipsi- and the contralateral subthalamic nucleus to the moved side.

claim: Only the synchronization in the gamma band showed a trend toward a more pronounced gamma ERS in the subthalamic nucleus contralateral to the moved limb (theta band: p=0.4, beta band: p=0.8, gamma band: p=0.08).
source: Only the synchronization in the gamma band showed a trend toward a more pronounced gamma ERS in the subthalamic nucleus contralateral to the moved limb (theta band: p=0.4, beta band: p=0.8, gamma band: p=0.08), as seen in Figure 2.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the comparison of ipsi- and contralateral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Large and medium movements entrain a significantly stronger gamma synchronization in the subthalamic nucleus contralateral rather than ipsilateral to the moved side (medium: p=0.01, large: p=0.03).
source: While large and medium movements entrain a significantly stronger gamma synchronization in the subthalamic nucleus contralateral rather than ipsilateral to the moved side, small movements go along with a similar oscillatory activity in both subthalamic nuclei (small: p=0.9, medium: p=0.01, large: p=0.03, permutation test) as shown in Figure 2E.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the comparison of ipsi- and contralateral data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Small movements go along with a similar oscillatory activity in both subthalamic nuclei (p=0.9).
source: While large and medium movements entrain a significantly stronger gamma synchronization in the subthalamic nucleus contralateral rather than ipsilateral to the moved side, small movements go along with a similar oscillatory activity in both subthalamic nuclei (small: p=0.9, medium: p=0.01, large: p=0.03, permutation test) as shown in Figure 2E.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the comparison of ipsi- and contralateral data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mean relative power changes were similar in both hemispheres for all conditions in the theta band (small: p=0.8, medium: p=0.4, large: p=0.5).

claim: Mean relative power changes were similar in both hemispheres for all conditions in the beta band (small: p=1, medium: p=1, large: p=0.5).

claim: Gamma-band activity was significantly stronger when aligned on maximal velocity (14.5%) compared to maximal amplitude (6.9%, p<0.001) and movement onset (12.3%, p=0.02).
source: Mean gamma power (0–0.5 s following the respective time point) was compared between the three alignment points. This revealed a significantly stronger synchronization in the gamma band when aligned on maximal velocity (14.5%) compared to maximal amplitude (6.9%, p<0.001) and movement onset (12.3%, p=0.02), see Figure 3.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the comparison of different alignment methods shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was a positive correlation between contralateral gamma band power (40–90 Hz, ±0.5 s around maximal velocity) and the maximally reached velocity on a single-trial level that was significant in 8/16 patients.

claim: A weak but significant positive correlation between relative power changes in the subthalamic nucleus contralateral to the moved hand and maximal velocity within a trial extended from 24 to 95 Hz and −400 to +600 ms around maximal velocity (p<0.05, FDR-corrected).

evidence: This is a statistical finding from single-trial correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The subthalamic nucleus ipsilateral to the movement side lacked correlation between velocity and relative power changes.

evidence: This is a finding from single-trial correlation analysis.

claim: The significant correlation between relative power changes and behavior on a single-trial level was specific for velocity.

evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mean gamma power correlated negatively with the individual UPDRS-ON score (Spearman's ρ = −0.55, p=0.038).
